Lee Young-jun has nothing left to gain. That is why South Korea are in the final

  • 기자명 HAN, June
  • 입력 2026.09.30 21:55
  • 댓글 0

SNS 기사보내기

이 기사를 공유합니다

The Grasshoppers striker finished his military service two years ago, yet it was he who dragged Lee Min-sung's side past China and within one match of a fourth straight Asian Games gold

 

There is a question that hangs over every South Korean squad at the Asian Games, and it is rarely about football. It is about who, come the final whistle of the final, will be spared 18 months of national service.

Lee Young-jun is not one of them. He enlisted with Gimcheon Sangmu, the army's football club, in January 2023 and walked out a sergeant in July 2024, a fortnight before signing for Grasshoppers in Zurich. A gold medal in Toyota on Saturday will earn him precisely nothing in exemptions. It will, one suspects, mean rather a lot more to him than that.

In Osaka on Wednesday afternoon, Lee was the man who hauled South Korea's under-23s back into a semi-final that was drifting away from them. China had gone ahead through Wang Yudong on 23 minutes, and the Nagai Stadium's Chinese contingent were making themselves heard. Ten minutes later Lee levelled from Eom Ji-sung's delivery. Bae Jun-ho, of Stoke City, won it with eight minutes remaining, again from an Eom assist. 2-1, and a place in the final secured.

Lee emerged from it with a cut on his chin. His first thought was for his team-mate. "Jun-ho's got a black eye," he offered, and then, unprompted, reeled off the damage elsewhere: "Jun-ho's eye is busted, Do-yoon had a nosebleed. Everyone is sacrificing themselves. I think I need to work harder."

It is an unusual thing to hear from the one man in the dressing room with no stake in the service question. It was not the first time he has made the point. After his brace in the 4-0 quarter-final win over Vietnam, a broadcaster asked him, with remarkable candour, why he was bothering to run so hard having already done his time. "You're wearing the national crest," Lee replied. "You don't take it easy just because you've done the army."

 

The shrug heard round Osaka

Wednesday's talking point, inevitably, was the celebration. Wang had marked China's opener with a rendition of the "BAD challenge" dance popularised by San of the K-pop group ATEEZ, a pointed choice on a Korean afternoon. Lee answered his own goal with arms spread and palms up, a theatrical "What, me?" that was read instantly as a riposte.

He insists it was nothing of the sort. "The Chinese fans were very loud," he said. "I didn't know their player had danced to provoke us. I only found out afterwards. It was about bringing the momentum back and lifting the team." A pause, and then the admission that rather gave the game away: "If I'd seen it, I'd probably have copied it."

On the refereeing, which left both camps grumbling, he was admirably unbothered. "That's football. The Chinese side will have complaints too. We won, so I suppose the referee was on our side."

Unfinished business

There is a symmetry here worth noting. Two and a half years ago, at the U-23 Asian Cup in Qatar, Lee scored twice against China in the group stage and was the most dangerous forward in the tournament. It ended in ignominy: sent off in the quarter-final against Indonesia, he watched South Korea lose on penalties and miss the Olympics for the first time in 40 years.

He very nearly missed this tournament too. A change of leadership at Grasshoppers left his release in limbo, and the Korea Football Association dispatched an official to Switzerland to negotiate. He arrived in Nagoya on 21 September and played the following evening against Saudi Arabia. Three goals in his last two matches suggest the journey took little out of him.

At 6ft 4in he is more than a target man. His hold-up play is what allows Eom, Bae and Celtic's Yang Hyun-jun to operate between the lines, and Lee Min-sung's winning move on Wednesday, which the striker said the manager had drilled in the dressing room, depended on him occupying centre-halves.

 

One more

South Korea, champions in 2014, 2018 and 2022, face the winner of Uzbekistan and hosts Japan on 3 October at the Toyota Stadium. Asked to put a figure on his side's chances, Lee did not hesitate. "One hundred per cent. I don't intend to lose even one per cent."

He would like a third successive goal, he conceded, but would trade it happily. "If we win, I don't care if I don't score. The team comes first."

His parents were in the stands on Wednesday, though he only glimpsed them from the pitch. He has promised to hang the medal around their necks before he flies back to Zurich. It is, when all is said and done, the only reward he is playing for.
